title: LeanQuant: Accurate and Scalable Large Language Model Quantization with Loss-error-aware Grid

raw.stage1:
### Purpose
The contribution's purpose is to identify why existing post-training quantization methods (e.g., GPTQ/OBQ) degrade accuracy and pinpoint their fundamental limitations. None of the prior papers explicitly report or establish the same empirical relationship between loss-error-based post-training quantization and accuracy degradation due to outliers in the inverse Hessian diagonal. While several papers (e.g., [6], [12], [22]) discuss outliers in quantization, they do not specifically analyze the connection between inverse Hessian outliers and task loss errors. Thus, the purpose is **not covered**.

### Mechanism
The mechanism involves analyzing how min-max affine quantization grids sacrifice weights corresponding to outliers in the inverse Hessian diagonal, leading to large task loss errors. Paper [30] discusses Hessian-aware quantization and uses second-order information (Hessian traces) for mixed-precision quantization, which is conceptually related to leveraging Hessian properties for quantization decisions. However, [30] does not address the specific mechanism of inverse Hessian diagonal outliers causing task loss errors in min-max affine grids. No other paper explicitly matches this mechanism. Thus, the mechanism is **not covered**.

### Evaluation
The evaluation involves qualitative visualization of min-max affine grids versus loss-error-aware grids for a specific LLM layer (e.g., Llama-3-8B). Paper [6] uses loss-error-aware grids for quantization and provides visualizations of quantization effects, which aligns with the evaluation design. Although the specific object (Llama-3-8B) differs, the evaluation design of visualizing quantization grids and their impact on loss is substantively equivalent. Thus, the evaluation is **covered**.

### Domain
The domain is large language models (LLMs), specifically post-training quantization for model compression. Numerous prior papers ([1], [2], [3], [5], [6], [8], [12], [22]) work in the same general application area of LLM post-training quantization and model compression. Although the specific sub-problem (inverse Hessian outliers in min-max affine grids) is new, the domain itself is well-covered. Thus, the domain is **covered**.

### Purpose
The contribution's purpose is to enable accurate quantization for extremely large-scale models (tens to hundreds of billions of parameters) while reducing memory and time overhead. Several prior papers address quantization for large language models (LLMs) to reduce memory and computational costs, but none explicitly focus on scaling quantization to models of this size with the same emphasis on reducing both memory and time overhead. For example, [1], [2], [3], [9], and [23] discuss quantization for LLMs but do not explicitly target the scalability to hundreds of billions of parameters or the specific reduction in both memory and time costs for such extreme scales. Therefore, the purpose appears to be novel.

### Mechanism
The mechanism involves designing and implementing a fused GPU kernel for grid learning, which parallelizes the enumeration search over S/Z candidate pairs (T=2048). This specific mechanism is not covered by prior work. While [8] discusses a fused kernel for W4A16 quantized inference and [17] and [21] discuss GPU kernel optimization and search, none of these papers describe a fused kernel specifically for grid learning or the parallelized enumeration of S/Z candidates. The mechanism is therefore novel.

### Evaluation
The evaluation demonstrates that the fused kernel achieves >50x end-to-end quantization speedup and successfully quantizes extremely large models (e.g., 123B and 405B parameters) on limited hardware, where prior methods fail due to out-of-memory (OOM) errors. While [8] evaluates fused kernels for quantized inference, and [23] and [25] evaluate post-training quantization methods, none of these papers use the same evaluation design of demonstrating quantization success and speedup at this extreme scale (e.g., 123B and 405B parameters) or compare against OOM failures of prior methods. The evaluation design appears to be novel.

### Domain
The domain is large language models (LLMs), specifically focusing on quantization and system efficiency. This domain is well-covered by prior work, including [1], [2], [3], [9], [12], [13], [14], [23], and [25], all of which address quantization and efficiency for LLMs. While the specific models and scales may differ, the general application area of LLM quantization and efficiency is not new.
